Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN) -- David and Christina Macfarlane always dreamed of opening a restaurant. And with David's background as a White House chef, they certainly have the in-house culinary ability. David and Christina Macfarlane in their Minneapolis restaurant, L'Ecosse. But they never imagined they'd be doing it in one of the toughest economic times ever, and they wondered if it would even be possible. "The banks were like, 'You're opening a restaurant now?' " Christina says. " 'Yeah, we're opening a restaurant now.' " David was born in Glasgow, Scotland, but moved to the United States with his family in his early teens and soon found his passion for the palate. Soon after high school, he joined the U.S. Navy, where he ultimately spent years cooking -- two of which were spent in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue as a chef for President Clinton at the beginning of his first term in 1992. Looking at a picture of himself and the former president, David describes a favorite memory. "He said that was the best meal he ever ate. I was pretty geeked about that."  See more about that favorite meal » . But the Macfarlanes wanted more time as a family -- something not suited to David's high-profile job. They moved a number of times before settling down in the Minneapolis, Minnesota, suburbs where, most recently, David worked for Fusion Culinary -- until his position was eliminated, that is. Christina says that as dismayed as David was over the job loss, she saw it as "a blessing." "I thought, 'Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!' " she says, adding that she saw it as the perfect opportunity to follow through with their dream. Now, despite the battered economy, the two stand behind the bar in their new restaurant, L'Ecosse, which, incidentally, is French for "Scotland." However, they have a slightly different take on the menu than perhaps they would have had if times were perkier. "We went to over a dozen restaurants looking at menus, pricepoints, [and] realizing the struggles in the economy," Christina recalls. The two concluded that while people are still eating out, they aren't seeking "fancy" food -- in other words, they weren't seeking the type of fare one might typically associate with state dinners at the White House. David says that's all a misconception anyway. "Comfort food," he says. "That's what the president wanted most." Some of the president's favorite foods, David says were nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, or just warm milk and cookies. "[President Clinton] wasn't looking for any of the fancy frou-frou stuff. We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but ... at lunchtime when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he'd say] 'Lemme have a tuna sandwich.' " At L'Ecosse, tuna and warm cookies are on the menu. Keeping with his Scottish upbringing, David's menu also is largely UK-centric: meat pies and fish and chips are two of the specialties. He does it all with fresh, local ingredients and says he can keep prices down because he does a lot of the work himself and with the help of a very minimal staff.  Watch the chef talk about keeping it simple » . Everything on the breakfast and lunch menus is priced under $10, and the two say that when they expand to a full dinner menu once their liquor license is approved, they want to keep prices similarly low. "The reason we did that was so nobody had sticker shock," David says. "They're very good items, but they're also inexpensive items and you're not going to break the bank." "If you want to come in and get Bill Clinton's favorite, it doesn't have to be $15 during the day. And that's what we want people to understand -- we understand where you're at." As Christina puts it, "You are going to get great food that your mother used to make for you." And, ideally, the bill won't send you into debt.

outputs.L1:
**MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN)** — David and Christina Macfarlane had always dreamed of opening a restaurant. With David’s background as a White House chef, they certainly had the culinary expertise. But they never imagined pursuing their dream during one of the toughest economic periods ever—and they wondered whether it would even be possible.

“The banks were like, ‘You’re opening a restaurant now?’” Christina says. “‘Yeah, we’re opening a restaurant now.’”

David was born in Glasgow, Scotland, but moved with his family to the United States in his early teens, where he soon discovered his passion for food. Shortly after high school, he joined the U.S. Navy and ultimately spent years cooking, including two years in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. There, he served as a chef for President Clinton at the beginning of Clinton’s first term in 1992.

Looking at a photograph of himself with the former president, David recalls a favorite memory.

“He said that was the best meal he ever ate. I was pretty geeked about that.”

*See more about that favorite meal »*

But the Macfarlanes wanted more time together as a family—something David’s high-profile job did not allow. They moved several times before settling in the suburbs of Minneapolis, Minnesota. Most recently, David worked for Fusion Culinary, until his position was eliminated.

Although David was dismayed by the job loss, Christina viewed it as “a blessing.”

“I thought, ‘Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!’” she says, adding that she saw it as the perfect opportunity to pursue their dream.

Now, despite the battered economy, the couple stands behind the bar of their new restaurant, L’Ecosse—French for “Scotland.” David and Christina Macfarlane are pictured in the Minneapolis restaurant.

Given the economic climate, however, they have taken a slightly different approach to the menu than they might have during more prosperous times.

“We went to over a dozen restaurants, looking at menus, price points, [and] realizing the struggles in the economy,” Christina recalls.

The couple concluded that although people were still dining out, they were not seeking “fancy” food—in other words, the kind of fare typically associated with White House state dinners. David says that perception is a misconception anyway.

“Comfort food,” he says. “That’s what the president wanted most.”

According to David, some of President Clinton’s favorite foods included nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, and warm milk and cookies.

“[President Clinton] wasn’t looking for any of the fancy frou-frou stuff. We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but ... at lunchtime, when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he’d say], ‘Lemme have a tuna sandwich.’”

At L’Ecosse, both tuna and warm cookies appear on the menu. Reflecting David’s Scottish upbringing, the menu is also largely UK-centric, with meat pies and fish and chips among the specialties.

David prepares everything with fresh, local ingredients. He says he can keep prices low because he does much of the work himself, with the help of a very small staff.

*Watch the chef talk about keeping it simple »*

Every item on the breakfast and lunch menus is priced under $10. Once the restaurant’s liquor license is approved and the Macfarlanes expand to a full dinner menu, they say they intend to keep those prices similarly low.

“The reason we did that was so nobody had sticker shock,” David says. “They’re very good items, but they’re also inexpensive items, and you’re not going to break the bank.”

“If you want to come in and get Bill Clinton’s favorite, it doesn’t have to be $15 during the day. And that’s what we want people to understand—we understand where you’re at.”

As Christina puts it, “You are going to get great food that your mother used to make for you.”

And, ideally, the bill will not send you into debt.

Not long after graduating from high school, he enlisted in the U.S. Navy and went on to spend years working as a cook. Two of those years were at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, where he served as one of President Bill Clinton’s chefs at the start of Clinton’s first term in 1992.

While looking at a photograph of himself with the former president, David remembers one especially meaningful moment: Clinton told him it was the best meal he had ever eaten. David says he was thrilled by the compliment. See more about that memorable meal » .

After relocating several times, they settled in the suburbs of Minneapolis. David’s most recent job was with Fusion Culinary, but the company eventually eliminated his position.

Although David was upset about losing his job, Christina regarded the setback as “a blessing.” She remembers thinking, “Thank you, Lord!” because she believed it gave them the ideal chance to finally pursue their restaurant dream.

Despite the weak economy, the couple now works behind the bar at L’Ecosse—a name that means “Scotland” in French. Economic conditions did, however, influence the kind of menu they created.

Christina says they visited more than a dozen restaurants, studying menus and prices while considering the financial pressures customers were facing. They determined that people were continuing to dine out but were not interested in elaborate cuisine, such as the food often associated with formal White House dinners.

According to David, however, the belief that presidents always want sophisticated meals is inaccurate. What Clinton preferred most, he says, was comfort food. Among the president’s favorites were nachos with salsa, tuna sandwiches, and warm milk served with cookies.

David explains that Clinton did not usually ask for ornate or overly fancy dishes. That type of cooking was reserved for state dinners and visiting dignitaries. When Clinton was alone in the Oval Office at lunchtime, he might simply request a tuna sandwich.

Both tuna and warm cookies appear on L’Ecosse’s menu. Reflecting David’s Scottish childhood, much of the restaurant’s food is also inspired by the United Kingdom, with meat pies and fish and chips among its specialties.

David uses fresh ingredients sourced locally. He says the restaurant can charge less because he handles much of the work himself and operates with only a very small staff. Watch the chef explain his straightforward approach » .

Every breakfast and lunch item costs less than $10. Once the restaurant receives its liquor license and introduces a complete dinner menu, David and Christina hope to keep evening prices comparably affordable.

David says they chose those prices to prevent customers from being startled by the bill. The dishes are high quality but inexpensive, he explains, so eating there should not strain anyone’s finances.

Customers who want to order one of Bill Clinton’s favorite meals should not have to pay $15 for it during the day, David adds. The couple wants diners to know that they understand the financial difficulties people are experiencing.

In Christina’s words, the restaurant offers excellent food like the meals customers’ mothers once prepared for them—and, ideally, the final check will not leave anyone in debt.

counterfactuals.output:
# From the White House to Minneapolis, a chef brings Scotland to the table

**Minneapolis, Minnesota** — At a time when many diners are watching every dollar, former White House chef David Macfarlane and his wife, Christina, are betting that comfort food, fair prices and a touch of Scottish hospitality can still bring people together.

The couple have opened an affordable Scottish restaurant in Minneapolis, trading the formality of presidential dining for a neighborhood room built around hearty meals and an unpretentious welcome.

For David Macfarlane, the move marks a striking change of scale. In the White House, food is shaped by protocol, precision and the expectations that accompany one of the world’s most prominent addresses. In Minneapolis, the mission is more immediate: serve satisfying dishes at prices local families can manage during an economic downturn.

That means leaning into the strengths of Scottish cooking — filling portions, practical ingredients and recipes designed to stretch modest staples without sacrificing flavor. The menu draws on familiar traditions, with savory pies, soups, potatoes and other warming dishes that feel especially suited to Minnesota winters.

Christina Macfarlane is central to the restaurant’s identity, helping create the sense that guests are entering a family-run establishment rather than a rarefied dining room. Together, the couple want the space to feel accessible to customers who may be curious about Scottish food but wary of expensive restaurants.

Opening during a downturn is a calculated risk. Restaurants face higher operating costs while customers are cutting discretionary spending, making affordability both a selling point and a challenge. The Macfarlanes’ approach is to keep the experience straightforward: recognizable ingredients, generous food and an atmosphere that does not require a special occasion.

Their timing may also work in their favor. When economic uncertainty rises, diners often seek comfort and value — qualities deeply rooted in the kind of food the couple are serving. Scottish cuisine, sometimes overshadowed in the United States by French, Italian or broader British fare, offers a natural fit for that mood.

The restaurant also gives Minneapolis diners a personal connection to a world far removed from Minnesota. David Macfarlane’s White House background brings distinction, but the couple are not positioning the business as an exercise in presidential nostalgia. Instead, they are using that experience in service of something more modest: consistency, hospitality and well-made everyday food.

In a difficult economy, the Macfarlanes are wagering that luxury is not the only thing culinary expertise can provide. Sometimes, it can mean a warm plate, a reasonable bill and a place where diners feel looked after.

For a chef who once cooked at the nation’s most famous residence, success now may be measured less by ceremony than by whether Minneapolis customers return — hungry, curious and ready for another taste of Scotland.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a human-interest news report about a laid-off chef who turns adversity into an opportunity by opening a restaurant with his wife, despite a difficult economy.
counterfactuals.output:
### Laid-Off Chef Finds Recipe for Renewal in Family-Run Restaurant

**RIVERTON —** When chef Daniel Morales lost his job last winter, he packed his knives into a worn canvas roll and left the hotel kitchen where he had worked for nearly a decade. Rising food costs and declining bookings had forced management to cut staff, leaving Morales unsure how he would support his family.

Six months later, those same knives are back at work in a kitchen of his own.

Morales, 42, and his wife, Elena, recently opened **Second Serving**, a 30-seat neighborhood restaurant specializing in affordable comfort food with Latin American influences. The couple financed the venture with their savings, a small business loan and help from relatives who contributed everything from paint to secondhand chairs.

“Losing my job felt like a door slamming shut,” Morales said as he prepared braised chicken for the dinner crowd. “Eventually, my wife said, ‘Maybe this is the push we’ve been waiting for.’”

Opening a restaurant is risky in any economy, but the Moraleses began their business as consumers were cutting back and restaurant owners were struggling with higher prices for food, utilities and labor.

To keep costs manageable, the couple leased a former sandwich shop that already had a working kitchen. Daniel designed a short menu that changes according to seasonal prices, while Elena handles the dining room, payroll and social media.

“We couldn’t afford waste,” Elena said. “Every ingredient had to be used wisely, and every purchase had to have a purpose.”

The menu reflects that philosophy. Slow-cooked pork appears in sandwiches at lunch and alongside rice and roasted vegetables at dinner. Vegetable trimmings become stock, while day-old bread is transformed into pudding. Most meals are priced below $18.

The restaurant’s name came from the couple’s belief that both food and people deserve another chance.

“This is our second serving,” Elena said. “It’s not the life we planned, but it may become something better.”

The first weeks were difficult. Some evenings brought only a handful of customers, and the couple worried they had misjudged the market. Daniel took occasional catering jobs to cover bills, while Elena continued part-time bookkeeping work.

Word began to spread after local residents posted photographs of the restaurant’s empanadas and cinnamon bread pudding online. Business has since grown steadily, particularly on weekends.

Regular customer Marsha Lee said the restaurant offers something many families are seeking: a meal that feels special without being unaffordable.

“You can tell they’re putting their whole heart into it,” Lee said. “People want to support that.”

The restaurant now employs four part-time workers, including two former colleagues of Daniel’s who also lost hospitality jobs. He hopes to add weekday breakfast service if sales remain strong.

For now, the couple measures success cautiously. They are not yet taking regular salaries, and unexpected expenses remain a constant concern. A broken refrigerator or another jump in food prices could quickly erase their narrow margin.

Still, Daniel said owning the restaurant has restored a sense of purpose he lost after being laid off.

“Before, I cooked someone else’s menu and worried someone else might decide I wasn’t needed,” he said. “Now every day is harder, but every plate feels like it belongs to us.”

As the dinner rush began on a recent Friday, Elena greeted customers at the door while Daniel called orders from the kitchen. Their 15-year-old daughter folded napkins at a corner table before taking a seat to do her homework.

The dining room filled slowly, then all at once.

Daniel paused at the kitchen window and looked out at the occupied tables.

“We’re still scared,” he said. “But we’re also hopeful. Sometimes those two things come together.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an article explaining how former presidential chef David Macfarlane used Bill Clinton’s preference for simple foods—such as tuna sandwiches, nachos, and cookies—to inspire the accessible menu at his new restaurant.
counterfactuals.output:
# From the White House to the Neighborhood Table: David Macfarlane’s Menu of Familiar Favorites

After cooking for a president, a chef might be expected to open a restaurant built around elaborate tasting menus and formal service. Former presidential chef David Macfarlane took a different path. For his new restaurant, he drew inspiration from Bill Clinton’s fondness for straightforward comfort foods—including tuna sandwiches, nachos, and cookies—to create a menu intended to feel familiar, affordable, and easy to enjoy.

Macfarlane’s experience in the White House showed him that influential guests do not always want complicated food. Despite the ceremony surrounding the presidency, everyday meals could be surprisingly simple. Clinton’s preferences demonstrated the appeal of dishes that are recognizable, satisfying, and free of unnecessary fuss.

That lesson became a guiding principle for Macfarlane’s restaurant. Rather than treating accessible foods as an afterthought, he placed them at the center of the concept. A tuna sandwich, for example, may be modest, but careful preparation and good ingredients can make it restaurant-worthy. Nachos offer the same opportunity: they are casual and communal, yet their quality depends on thoughtful layering, balanced toppings, and attention to texture. Cookies provide a similarly universal pleasure, ending a meal with something nostalgic rather than ornate.

The approach reflects a broader idea about hospitality. Diners do not always need to be challenged or impressed by unfamiliar techniques; often, they want food that makes them comfortable. Macfarlane’s White House background gives him the technical foundation to refine familiar dishes without stripping away what people love about them.

Clinton’s preferences also helped bridge the distance between presidential dining and ordinary life. While the White House is associated with state dinners and formal banquets, a president may still crave the same quick lunch or late-night snack as anyone else. By translating that insight into his restaurant, Macfarlane has made his high-level culinary experience feel approachable rather than exclusive.

The result is a menu shaped less by prestige than by pleasure. Tuna sandwiches, nachos, and cookies may not sound presidential in the traditional sense, but that is precisely the point. Macfarlane learned that simple food can carry as much appeal as an elaborate plate—and that good cooking is often about giving familiar favorites the care they deserve.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN restaurant profile covering L’Ecosse’s Scottish-inspired dishes, local ingredients, under-$10 pricing, minimal staffing, and the owners’ struggle to launch the business during a recession.
counterfactuals.output:
### L’Ecosse serves Scottish flavor on a recession-era budget

At L’Ecosse, Scottish tradition meets the realities of running a small restaurant in a difficult economy.

The menu draws inspiration from Scotland’s hearty, unpretentious cooking, while relying on ingredients sourced from nearby farms and producers whenever possible. Instead of costly imports or elaborate presentation, the owners focus on familiar, satisfying dishes that showcase local meat, vegetables and baked goods.

Affordability is central to the concept. Most items cost less than $10, a deliberate choice aimed at making the restaurant accessible to diners watching their spending.

Keeping prices low requires an equally lean operation. L’Ecosse runs with minimal staffing, leaving the owners to handle many of the daily responsibilities themselves—from preparing food and serving customers to ordering supplies and cleaning up after closing.

Launching the business during a recession made an already risky venture even harder. Financing was scarce, customers were cautious and every expense had to be scrutinized. The owners responded by starting small, limiting overhead and building the restaurant around ingredients available close to home.

Their struggle reflects the challenge facing many independent restaurants: balancing quality and fair prices while surviving on narrow margins. For L’Ecosse, that means combining Scottish-inspired comfort food, local sourcing and a hands-on approach—one under-$10 plate at a time.
